Game: Two shuffles, f and g, are done one after the other. The third picture shows the single shuffle that does the same.
How to play: Press two numbers in f or in g to swap them and watch the third picture change.

Look for the math

Doing one shuffle after another is itself a shuffle. If f is done first and g second, the product fg sends k to g(f(k)). The page uses this left-to-right order, and so does this one.

Reading the product

To find where k goes in fg, follow the arrow from k in the first picture to f(k), then the arrow from that number in the second. The test compared the picture with this rule for every pair of permutations of up to 5 numbers.

Order matters

With two numbers fg = gf always, but with three or more it often is not: the test found pairs with fg ≠ gf for every N from 3 to 5. Still, (fg)h = f(gh) always (checked up to 4 numbers), the do-nothing shuffle is a unit, and every permutation has an inverse with (fg)-1 = g-1f-1. These facts make the permutations a group.

Swaps and parity

Pressing two numbers multiplies a permutation by their transposition. Each swap flips whether a permutation is even or odd, and the test confirmed that sign(fg) = sign(f)·sign(g) for all pairs: an even and an odd permutation always give an odd product, and two odd ones give an even product.

Swap two numbers in f and see which arrows of the product change. How many are they?
